These analyses follow the review in `suggested_edits.md` (sections A, B, F and G). They use the same data,
exclusions and main model as the paper (`_00_data_prep.qmd`, `_02_angle_sensitivity.qmd`). The IRT checks
(sections 3 to 5) are fit in `../03_irt_checks.qmd` and the scripts in `checks/`, and read from `models/`.
Sections 1 and 2 cover the 2D/3D comparison and accuracy; 3 and 4 dimensionality and DIF; 5 the effect of priors on the
invariance comparison and the reliability values; 6 further response-time checks (adaptive format, exemplars, age, site by age);
and 7 sex differences.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(here)
library(lme4)
library(performance)
library(marginaleffects)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
```

{{< include _00_data_prep.qmd >}}

{{< include _02_angle_sensitivity.qmd >}}

```{r helpers}
fmt3 <- \(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
fmt2 <- \(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pct <- \(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 1), "%")
ci_str <- \(lo, hi, f = fmt3) glue("[{f(lo)}, {f(hi)}]")
site_order <- c("mpieva-de", "uniandes-co-bogota", "uniandes-co-rural", "western-ca")
```

# 1. Does the angle effect differ between 2D and 3D stimuli?

The main model pools stimulus types when reporting the overall angle slope, and `_02` compares 2D and 3D
slopes only across all sites together. Here the comparison is made within each site. As in the main text,
the contrast is restricted to the angles both types were administered at (40°, 80°, 120°), because 3D items
were never given at 160° and the angle function is not linear. The model is the main model fitted to those
angles, with stimulus type (2D/3D) in place of the three-level stimulus factor so that the 2D/3D slope
difference is a single parameter; slopes are average marginal effects over the observed trials.

```{r dim-models}
shared_data <- mrot_lme_data |>
  filter(angle %in% shared_angles) |>
  mutate(angle_sc = (angle - mean(angle)) / deg)
contrasts(shared_data$site_label) <- contr.sum(levels(shared_data$site_label))
contrasts(shared_data$item_group) <- contr.sum(levels(shared_data$item_group))

ctl <- lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
m_ig <- lmer(log_rt ~ angle_sc * item_group * site_label * age_sc +
               trial_number * item_group + adaptive * item_group +
               (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
             data = shared_data, REML = FALSE, control = ctl)

# likelihood-ratio tests of the 3D-2D slope difference
m_no_site <- update(m_ig, . ~ . - angle_sc:item_group:site_label - angle_sc:item_group:site_label:age_sc)
m_no_age  <- update(m_ig, . ~ . - angle_sc:item_group:age_sc - angle_sc:item_group:site_label:age_sc)
m_no_diff <- update(m_ig, . ~ . - angle_sc:item_group - angle_sc:item_group:site_label -
                      angle_sc:item_group:age_sc - angle_sc:item_group:site_label:age_sc)
lrt <- \(small) { a <- anova(small, m_ig); tibble(chisq = a$Chisq[2], df = a$Df[2], p = a[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]) }
lrt_site <- lrt(m_no_site)
lrt_age  <- lrt(m_no_age)
lrt_any  <- lrt(m_no_diff)

slopes_ig <- slopes(m_ig, newdata = shared_data, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
                    by = c("item_group", "site_label")) |> as_tibble()
diff_site <- slopes(m_ig, newdata = shared_data, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
                    by = c("item_group", "site_label"), hypothesis = ~ pairwise | site_label) |> as_tibble()
diff_all <- slopes(m_ig, newdata = shared_data, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
                   by = "item_group", hypothesis = ~ pairwise) |> as_tibble()

shared_data_age <- shared_data |> mutate(age_group = cut(age, age_breaks, right = FALSE))
diff_age <- slopes(m_ig, newdata = shared_data_age, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
                   by = c("item_group", "age_group"), hypothesis = ~ pairwise | age_group) |> as_tibble()

# slopes over each type's own range, from the main model (for comparison)
slopes_full <- slopes(full_mod, newdata = mrot_lme_data, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
                      by = c("item_group", "site_label")) |> as_tibble()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-2d3d
#| tbl-cap: "**Angle slope (log RT per 40°) by stimulus type and site.** Common angles: 40°, 80° and 120° only, from the model described above. Own range: each type over the angles it received (2D up to 160°, 3D up to 120°), from the main model. The last column is the 3D minus 2D difference on the common angles."

tab <- slopes_ig |>
  transmute(site_label, item_group, common = glue("{fmt3(estimate)} {ci_str(conf.low, conf.high)}")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = item_group, values_from = common, names_prefix = "common_")
tab_full <- slopes_full |>
  transmute(site_label, item_group, own = fmt3(estimate)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = item_group, values_from = own, names_prefix = "own_")
tab_diff <- diff_site |>
  transmute(site_label, diff = glue("{fmt3(estimate)} {ci_str(conf.low, conf.high)}, p {map_chr(p.value, fmt_p)}"))
overall <-slopes(m_ig, newdata = shared_data, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "item_group") |> as_tibble()
overall_row <- tibble(site_label = "All sites",
                      common_2d = glue("{fmt3(overall$estimate[overall$item_group == '2d'])} {ci_str(overall$conf.low[overall$item_group == '2d'], overall$conf.high[overall$item_group == '2d'])}"),
                      common_3d = glue("{fmt3(overall$estimate[overall$item_group == '3d'])} {ci_str(overall$conf.low[overall$item_group == '3d'], overall$conf.high[overall$item_group == '3d'])}"),
                      own_2d = fmt3(slope("2d")$estimate), own_3d = fmt3(slope("3d")$estimate),
                      diff = glue("{fmt3(diff_all$estimate)} {ci_str(diff_all$conf.low, diff_all$conf.high)}, p {fmt_p(diff_all$p.value)}"))
tab |>
  left_join(tab_full, by = "site_label") |>
  left_join(tab_diff, by = "site_label") |>
  mutate(site_label = factor(site_label, levels = site_order)) |> arrange(site_label) |>
  mutate(site_label = as.character(site_label)) |>
  bind_rows(overall_row) |>
  select(Site = site_label, `2D (common)` = common_2d, `3D (common)` = common_3d,
         `2D (own range)` = own_2d, `3D (own range)` = own_3d, `3D − 2D (common)` = diff) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-2d3d
#| fig-cap: "**Angle slopes for 2D and 3D stimuli at each site** (common angles 40--120°; points are average marginal effects, bars 95% CIs)."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.2

slopes_ig |>
  mutate(site_label = factor(site_label, levels = rev(site_order)),
         item_group = str_to_upper(item_group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, site_label, colour = item_group)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = "Angle slope (log RT per 40°)", y = NULL, colour = "Stimulus type") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

On the common angles the 3D slope is steeper than the 2D slope overall
(`{r} fmt3(diff_all$estimate)`, 95% CI `{r} ci_str(diff_all$conf.low, diff_all$conf.high)`,
*p* `{r} fmt_p(diff_all$p.value)`), but this difference is not uniform across sites
(likelihood-ratio test of the angle × stimulus type × site terms: χ²(`{r} lrt_site$df`) = `{r} fmt2(lrt_site$chisq)`,
*p* `{r} fmt_p(lrt_site$p)`). It is large at mpieva-de
(`{r} fmt3(diff_site$estimate[diff_site$site_label == "mpieva-de"])`, *p* `{r} fmt_p(diff_site$p.value[diff_site$site_label == "mpieva-de"])`)
and indistinguishable from zero at the other three sites (@tbl-2d3d). Whether the 2D/3D slope difference
changes with age is not clear (angle × stimulus type × age terms: χ²(`{r} lrt_age$df`) = `{r} fmt2(lrt_age$chisq)`,
*p* `{r} fmt_p(lrt_age$p)`; the contrast is `{r} fmt3(diff_age$estimate[1])`, `{r} fmt3(diff_age$estimate[2])` and `{r} fmt3(diff_age$estimate[3])` in the three age groups).
Both stimulus types show a clear positive angle slope at every site, so the finding that
response times increase with angle holds for each type separately.

# 2. Accuracy and the angle effect

The paper analyses response time on correct trials only. Accuracy as a function of angle is the other
standard dependent variable in mental rotation research and is needed to interpret the response-time results.

```{r acc-data}
acc <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  mutate(item_group = factor(item_group), site_label = factor(site_label),
         adaptive = factor(adaptive),
         angle_sc = (angle - mean(angle)) / deg, age_sc = (age - mean(age)) / yrs,
         correct = as.integer(correct), task = "mrot",
         age_group = cut(age, breaks = age_breaks, right = FALSE))
contrasts(acc$site_label) <- contr.sum(levels(acc$site_label))
contrasts(acc$item_group) <- contr.sum(levels(acc$item_group))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-acc-desc
#| tbl-cap: "**Proportion correct by stimulus type, angle and age group** (all valid trials; chance = .50)."

acc |>
  summarise(p = mean(correct), n = n(), .by = c(item_group, angle, age_group)) |>
  mutate(item_group = str_to_upper(item_group), p = fmt2(p)) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = age_group, values_from = p, names_sort = TRUE) |>
  arrange(item_group, angle) |>
  rename(`Stimulus type` = item_group, `Angle (°)` = angle) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE)
```

The accuracy model is a logistic mixed model with the same fixed effects as the response-time model
(angle × stimulus type × site × age, plus trial number and administration format × stimulus type) and
participant-level random intercepts and angle slopes. It was fit with `nAGQ = 0` (the default adaptive
quadrature did not finish in reasonable time); slopes are average marginal effects on the probability scale,
i.e. the change in proportion correct per 40° of rotation.

```{r acc-model}
acc_mod <- glmer(correct ~ angle_sc * item_group * site_label * age_sc + trial_number +
                   adaptive * item_group + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
                 data = acc, family = binomial, nAGQ = 0,
                 control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5)))

acc_slope <- \(by, nd = acc, mod = acc_mod) {
  slopes(mod, newdata = nd, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = by) |> as_tibble()
}
acc_by_type <- acc_slope("item_group")
acc_by_site <- acc_slope(c("item_group", "site_label"))
acc_by_age  <- acc_slope(c("item_group", "age_group"))
acc_diff_site <- slopes(acc_mod, newdata = acc, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
                        by = c("item_group", "site_label"), hypothesis = ~ pairwise | site_label) |> as_tibble()
acc_overall <- slopes(acc_mod, newdata = acc, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "task") |> as_tibble()

# the same model on fixed-form (non-adaptive) runs only: adaptive item selection ties angle to ability
acc_fixed <- acc |> filter(adaptive == "FALSE") |> droplevels()
contrasts(acc_fixed$site_label) <- contr.sum(levels(acc_fixed$site_label))
contrasts(acc_fixed$item_group) <- contr.sum(levels(acc_fixed$item_group))
acc_mod_fixed <- glmer(correct ~ angle_sc * item_group * site_label * age_sc + trial_number +
                         (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
                       data = acc_fixed, family = binomial, nAGQ = 0,
                       control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5)))
acc_by_type_fixed <- acc_slope("item_group", acc_fixed, acc_mod_fixed)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-acc-slopes
#| tbl-cap: "**Change in proportion correct per 40° of rotation** (average marginal effects, 95% CI). Negative values mean accuracy falls as the angle increases."

bind_rows(
  acc_by_type |> transmute(Level = "Stimulus type", Group = str_to_upper(item_group), estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
  acc_by_site |> transmute(Level = "Site", Group = glue("{str_to_upper(item_group)}, {site_label}"), estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
  acc_by_age  |> transmute(Level = "Age group", Group = glue("{str_to_upper(item_group)}, {as.character(age_group)}"), estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
) |>
  mutate(`Slope [95% CI]` = glue("{fmt3(estimate)} {ci_str(conf.low, conf.high)}")) |>
  select(Level, Group, `Slope [95% CI]`) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "l", "r"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-acc
#| fig-cap: "**Proportion correct by angle, stimulus type and age group.** Points are observed proportions with 95% binomial confidence intervals; the dashed line is chance."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6

acc |>
  summarise(k = sum(correct), n = n(), .by = c(item_group, angle, age_group)) |>
  mutate(p = k / n, se = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n),
         item_group = str_to_upper(item_group)) |>
  ggplot(aes(angle, p, colour = item_group)) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(age_group), labeller = labeller(.cols = \(x) paste("Age (years):", x))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = p - 1.96 * se, ymax = p + 1.96 * se), size = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(20, 40, 80, 120, 160)) +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (°)", y = "Proportion correct", colour = "Stimulus type") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Accuracy fell with rotation angle: by `{r} fmt3(-acc_overall$estimate)` in proportion correct per 40° overall
(95% CI `{r} ci_str(-acc_overall$conf.high, -acc_overall$conf.low)`), and for both 2D
(`{r} fmt3(-acc_by_type$estimate[acc_by_type$item_group == "2d"])`) and 3D items
(`{r} fmt3(-acc_by_type$estimate[acc_by_type$item_group == "3d"])`; @tbl-acc-slopes). The negative slope
was present at every site for both stimulus types. On fixed-form runs only, where item selection does not depend on
performance, the slopes were similar (2D `{r} fmt3(-acc_by_type_fixed$estimate[acc_by_type_fixed$item_group == "2d"])`,
3D `{r} fmt3(-acc_by_type_fixed$estimate[acc_by_type_fixed$item_group == "3d"])`). Accuracy was
well above chance on average, but 3D accuracy in 5--7-year-olds was only
`{r} pct(mean(acc$correct[acc$item_group == "3d" & acc$age_group == "[5,8)"]))`.
The speed and accuracy results therefore point the same way: larger rotations are slower and less accurate,
with no sign of a speed--accuracy trade-off across angles.

## Do fast guesses drive the age effect on the angle slope?

Because the task is two-alternative, correct trials include lucky guesses. Responses under 0.5 s were at
chance (2D: `{r} pct(mean(acc$correct[acc$item_group == "2d" & acc$rt_s < 0.5]))`;
3D: `{r} pct(mean(acc$correct[acc$item_group == "3d" & acc$rt_s < 0.5]))`), and they make up
`{r} pct(mean(acc$rt_s < 0.5))` of trials. If younger children guess quickly on hard items, their response-time slope would be
flattened, which could produce the age gradient in the angle slope without any difference in rotation.
To check, the main model was refit after removing fast responses, after keeping only runs with accuracy
significantly above chance (one-sided binomial test, *p* < .05), and on fixed-form runs only.

```{r rt-sensitivity}
run_acc <- acc |>
  summarise(k = sum(correct), n = n(), .by = run_id) |>
  mutate(above_chance = map2_dbl(k, n, \(k, n) binom.test(k, n, 0.5, alternative = "greater")$p.value) < .05)

fit_rt_sens <- function(d, label) {
  d <- d |> mutate(angle_sc = (angle - mean(angle)) / deg, age_sc = (age - mean(age)) / yrs,
                   site_label = droplevels(site_label), stimulus = droplevels(stimulus),
                   adaptive = droplevels(adaptive),
                   age_group = cut(age, breaks = age_breaks, right = FALSE))
  contrasts(d$site_label) <- contr.sum(nlevels(d$site_label))
  contrasts(d$stimulus) <- contr.sum(nlevels(d$stimulus))
  f <- if (nlevels(d$adaptive) > 1) {
    log_rt ~ angle_sc * stimulus * site_label * age_sc + trial_number * stimulus +
      adaptive * stimulus + (1 + angle_sc | user_id)
  } else {
    log_rt ~ angle_sc * stimulus * site_label * age_sc + trial_number * stimulus +
      (1 + angle_sc | user_id)
  }
  m <- lmer(f, data = d, REML = FALSE, control = ctl)
  by_age <- slopes(m, newdata = d, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "age_group") |> as_tibble()
  stopifnot(as.character(by_age$age_group) == c("[5,8)", "[8,11)", "[11,14)"))
  gp <- slopes(m, newdata = d, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "age_group",
               hypothesis = "b3 - b1 = 0") |> as_tibble()
  tibble(analysis = label, trials = nrow(d), children = n_distinct(d$user_id),
         s_young = by_age$estimate[1], s_mid = by_age$estimate[2], s_old = by_age$estimate[3],
         gap = gp$estimate, gap_se = gp$std.error, gap_p = gp$p.value)
}

rt_sens <- bind_rows(
  fit_rt_sens(mrot_lme_data, "Main model (as reported)"),
  fit_rt_sens(mrot_lme_data |> filter(rt_s >= 0.5), "Exclude responses < 0.5 s"),
  fit_rt_sens(mrot_lme_data |> filter(rt_s >= 1), "Exclude responses < 1 s"),
  fit_rt_sens(mrot_lme_data |> semi_join(run_acc |> filter(above_chance), by = "run_id"),
              "Only runs above chance"),
  fit_rt_sens(mrot_lme_data |> filter(adaptive == "FALSE"), "Fixed-form runs only")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rt-sens
#| tbl-cap: "**Angle slope (log RT per 40°) by age group under alternative exclusions.** The last column is the 11--13 minus 5--7 year-old difference (SE)."

rt_sens |>
  mutate(gap_txt = glue("{fmt3(gap)} ({fmt3(gap_se)}), p {map_chr(gap_p, fmt_p)}"),
         across(starts_with("s_"), fmt3), trials = format(trials, big.mark = ",")) |>
  select(Analysis = analysis, Trials = trials, Children = children,
         `5--7` = s_young, `8--10` = s_mid, `11--13` = s_old, `Difference` = gap_txt) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The age gradient survives each of these exclusions: the slope rises from `{r} fmt2(rt_sens$s_young[1])` to
`{r} fmt2(rt_sens$s_old[1])` across the age groups in the main model, and the oldest-minus-youngest difference stays
between `{r} fmt3(min(rt_sens$gap))` and `{r} fmt3(max(rt_sens$gap))` across all analyses (@tbl-rt-sens),
significant in each. It is smallest when only runs above chance are kept
(`{r} fmt3(rt_sens$gap[rt_sens$analysis == "Only runs above chance"])`), so guessing probably accounts for part of the gradient but not all of it.

# 3. Dimensionality

The paper's IRT models assume one latent factor. The supplement shows that 3D items differ from 2D items in
difficulty and discrimination, so the model was compared with two alternatives (fit in `../03_irt_checks.qmd`):
two correlated factors, one for 2D items and one for 3D items; and a general factor with an additional 3D-specific factor.
All are multigroup and scalar-invariant, with the paper's priors.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dim
#| tbl-cap: "**Fit of one- and two-dimensional scalar 2PL models.** ΔBIC is relative to the best-fitting model."

dim_res <- read_rds(here("models/mrot_dim.rds"))
dim_res$fit |>
  mutate(across(c(logLik, AIC, BIC, d_BIC), \(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1))) |>
  select(Model = model, Parameters = n_pars, `Log-lik.` = logLik, AIC, BIC, `ΔBIC` = d_BIC) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

```{r dim-values}
d1 <- dim_res$fit |> filter(model == "One factor")
d2 <- dim_res$fit |> filter(str_starts(model, "Two"))
d3 <- dim_res$fit |> filter(str_starts(model, "General"))
cor_range <- range(dim_res$cor$r_2d_3d)
```

Both multidimensional models fit better than the one-factor model by a wide margin (@tbl-dim): BIC is
`{r} round(d1$BIC - d2$BIC)` points lower for the two-factor model and `{r} round(d1$BIC - d3$BIC)` points lower for the
general-plus-3D-specific model. The estimated correlation between the 2D and 3D factors is moderate and varies by dataset
(`{r} fmt2(cor_range[1])` to `{r} fmt2(cor_range[2])`; mpieva-de, where the factor variances are fixed at 1, has the lowest).
In the general-plus-3D model, 3D items load on both the general factor and the specific factor. So the 3D items share
variance with the 2D items but not all of it, and a single θ conflates the two. This does not undermine the ordering of
children on the task as a whole, but it limits how far "mental rotation ability" can be treated as one dimension, and it bears on
the interpretation of the θ results (age and sex) in the paper. Note that dimensionality here is confounded with stimulus
type: the 3D items also differ in depth cues, visual complexity and familiarity, so the second factor may reflect any of these.

# 4. Differential item functioning

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dif
#| tbl-cap: "**Likelihood-ratio DIF tests across the four datasets.** Each item class is freed in turn (slope and intercept free across datasets; df = 6) and compared with the all-invariant model. Holm-adjusted *p* across the 12 tests. Difficulty (b) is the intercept divided by the slope, by dataset (mpieva-de / uniandes-co-bogota / uniandes-co-rural / western-ca)."

dif_res <- read_rds(here("models/mrot_dif.rds"))
dif_tab <- \(d) d |>
  mutate(b_by_group = map_chr(est, \(e) paste(fmt2(e$b), collapse = " / ")),
         item = str_remove(item, "^mrot_") |> str_replace_all("_", " ")) |>
  transmute(Item = item, `χ²(6)` = fmt2(chisq), `p (Holm)` = formatC(p_holm, format = "f", digits = 3), `b by dataset` = b_by_group)

kable(dif_tab(dif_res$two), booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Two-factor model (2D and 3D factors)")
kable(dif_tab(dif_res$uni), booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "One-factor model (as in the paper)")
```

```{r dif-values}
n_sig <- \(d) sum(d$p_holm < .05)
sig_items <- \(d) d |> filter(p_holm < .05) |> pull(item) |> str_remove("^mrot_") |> str_replace_all("_", " ")
```

Under the paper's one-factor model, `{r} n_sig(dif_res$uni)` of 12 item classes show DIF after Holm correction, and the
three 3D classes show it most strongly. Much of this comes from the one-factor model being misspecified: once 2D and 3D items
load on separate factors, `{r} n_sig(dif_res$two)` classes remain flagged (`{r} paste(sig_items(dif_res$two), collapse = ", ")`).
The remaining differences in difficulty are modest. For the flagged 3D 40° class, difficulty ranges from
`{r} fmt2(min(dif_res$two$est[[which(dif_res$two$item == "mrot_3d_shape_040")]]$b))` to
`{r} fmt2(max(dif_res$two$est[[which(dif_res$two$item == "mrot_3d_shape_040")]]$b))` across datasets, on a θ scale where the reference dataset (mpieva-de) has SD 1. Some freed slopes are very large in sparse cells (for example 7.1 for the 2D duck 40° class at
uniandes-co-rural), because the fits are unpenalised, so the individual estimates are unstable. With about 1,500 assessments the tests can also detect
small differences. These results flag items worth inspecting. They are not a final DIF classification, and partial invariance
(freeing the flagged classes) would be the natural next model.


# 5. Invariance, priors and reliability

## Do the priors drive the Table 3 comparison?

The paper's models carry priors on every item slope (N(1, 0.3)) and intercept (N(0, 3)). Table 3 compares
penalised log-likelihoods across invariance levels. The configural model has four times as many slope and intercept
parameters as the scalar model, and so pays four times as much prior penalty, which can make it look worse than a
nested, more constrained model. To check, the configural and scalar models were refit with and without the priors
(`checks/irt_priors_configural.R`). The configural model fixes each dataset's mean at 0 and variance at 1, as in the paper.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior
#| tbl-cap: "**Configural and scalar 2PL models with and without the priors.** Log-likelihoods are of the data alone. The no-prior configural model had not fully converged after 6,000 EM cycles, so its log-likelihood is a lower bound."

prior_res <- read_rds(here("models/mrot_prior.rds"))
prior_res$fit |>
  transmute(Model = model, Converged = if_else(converged, "yes", "no"), Parameters = n_pars,
            `Log-lik.` = formatC(logLik, format = "f", digits = 1),
            AIC = formatC(AIC, format = "f", digits = 1), BIC = formatC(BIC, format = "f", digits = 1)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

```{r prior-values}
pf <- prior_res$fit
get_fit <- \(m, col) pf[[col]][pf$model == m]
fi <- \(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = "")
cfg_p <- "Configural, with priors (paper)"; cfg_n <- "Configural, no priors"
sc_p <- "Scalar, with priors (paper)"; sc_n <- "Scalar, no priors"
```

The configural model with the priors has a log-likelihood of `{r} fmt2(get_fit(cfg_p, "logLik"))`, matching the paper's
Table 3, and it is `{r} round(get_fit(cfg_p, "logLik") - get_fit(sc_p, "logLik"))` points higher than the scalar model's, as it should be for a nested model.
(The paper's metric model, which sits between the two, has a log-likelihood of −21579, higher than the configural model's. This should not happen
either, and is consistent with the same prior penalty acting on the configural model, but the metric model was not refit here.)
But the priors cost the configural model about `{r} round(get_fit(cfg_n, "logLik") - get_fit(cfg_p, "logLik"))` log-likelihood
points and the scalar model about `{r} round(get_fit(sc_n, "logLik") - get_fit(sc_p, "logLik"))`.
Without the priors, a likelihood-ratio test rejects exact scalar invariance (χ²(`{r} prior_res$lrt$df`) = `{r} round(prior_res$lrt$chisq)`,
p < .001), and AIC prefers the configural model (`{r} fi(get_fit(cfg_n, "AIC"))` against `{r} fi(get_fit(sc_n, "AIC"))`).
BIC still prefers the scalar model, but by `{r} round(get_fit(cfg_n, "BIC") - get_fit(sc_n, "BIC"))` points, not the
`{r} round(get_fit(cfg_p, "BIC") - get_fit(sc_p, "BIC"))` reported with the priors.
So the claim that the data are more consistent with invariant parameters than with free parameters under BIC survives, but the large
margin partly reflects the priors, and "full" scalar invariance is not supported by an unpenalised likelihood-ratio test.
The DIF results in section 4 show where the departures are concentrated.

## Marginal reliability

The reliabilities in the paper (2PL: 0.73--0.89; Rasch: 0.31--0.34) come from `mirt::marginal_rxx` applied to each dataset's group model.
That function integrates `TI / (TI + var)` against a standard normal density, where `TI` is the test information and `var` is the fitted
latent variance of the group. Dataset variances are not 1 in the scalar models (the reference group has variance 1; the others
are larger, and in the Rasch model all are around 5--6, because the slopes are fixed at 1 while the data support slopes near 2).
The formula is therefore not invariant to the scale of θ, so the values depend on the arbitrary scaling of each model.
The scale-free alternatives below are the reliability for θ distributed N(mean, var), `var·TI / (var·TI + 1)`,
and the empirical reliability from the EAP scores (`mirt::empirical_rxx`). They were computed from the saved model records
(`checks/irt_reliability_records.R`). The paper's values are from the `all_items` models (81 item instances); Table 3 uses the
`overlap_items` models (54 instances).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rxx
#| tbl-cap: "**Marginal reliability of the scalar models by dataset under three definitions.** *mirt*: `marginal_rxx` as used in the paper. Corrected: variance-scaled reliability for θ ~ N(mean, var). Empirical: from EAP scores and their standard errors."

rxx_res <- read_rds(here("models/mrot_rxx_check.rds")) |>
  mutate(group = str_remove_all(group, "^pilot_|_main$") |> str_replace_all("_", "-"),
         itemtype = recode(itemtype, `2pl` = "2PL", rasch = "Rasch"),
         subset = recode(subset, all_items = "All items (as reported)", overlap_items = "Overlap items (Table 3)"))
rxx_res |>
  transmute(`Item set` = subset, Model = itemtype, Dataset = group,
            `Latent var.` = fmt2(var_theta), mirt = fmt2(rxx_mirt),
            Corrected = fmt2(rxx_density_corrected), Empirical = fmt2(rxx_empirical)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

```{r rxx-values}
rr <- \(ss, it, col) range(rxx_res[[col]][rxx_res$subset == ss & rxx_res$itemtype == it])
ao <- "All items (as reported)"
```

Under the scale-free definitions the Rasch and 2PL models are about equally reliable (all items, corrected:
2PL `{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "2PL", "rxx_density_corrected")[1])`--`{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "2PL", "rxx_density_corrected")[2])`,
Rasch `{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "Rasch", "rxx_density_corrected")[1])`--`{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "Rasch", "rxx_density_corrected")[2])`;
empirical: 2PL `{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "2PL", "rxx_empirical")[1])`--`{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "2PL", "rxx_empirical")[2])`,
Rasch `{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "Rasch", "rxx_empirical")[1])`--`{r} fmt2(rr(ao, "Rasch", "rxx_empirical")[2])`).
The 0.32 versus 0.89 contrast in the paper is a scaling artefact, not evidence that the 2PL measures more reliably.
The better fit of the 2PL over the Rasch model rests on the likelihood criteria alone.
Reliability is substantial for both: roughly 0.8--0.9 once children are scored on the same items.

# 6. Further checks on the response-time models

## Does the angle slope differ between adaptive and fixed-form runs?

The paper's check fits `log_rt ~ angle * adaptive` with no other covariates. Here the interaction is added to the full model
instead, so that it is estimated alongside the stimulus, site and age terms.

```{r adaptive-interaction}
m_ad <- update(full_mod, . ~ . + angle_sc:adaptive)
ad_lrt <- anova(full_mod, m_ad)
ad_coef <- summary(m_ad)$coefficients[str_detect(rownames(summary(m_ad)$coefficients), "^angle_sc:adaptive"), , drop = FALSE]
```

The adaptive × angle coefficient is `{r} fmt3(ad_coef[1, 1])` (SE = `{r} fmt3(ad_coef[1, 2])`, *t* = `{r} fmt2(ad_coef[1, 3])`;
likelihood-ratio χ²(1) = `{r} fmt2(ad_lrt$Chisq[2])`, *p* = `{r} fmt3(ad_lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2])`).
The adaptive slope is flatter. The estimate is imprecise and close to the conventional threshold, which is different from
"no difference". The paper's simple model gives
Δβ = `{r} fmt3(cat_slope_diff$estimate)` (SE = `{r} fmt3(cat_slope_diff$std.error)`), with the opposite sign. The row for `adaptive`
in Table 4 of the paper contrasts marginal slopes of a model that has no adaptive × angle term, so it reflects which sites, stimuli and
ages used each format and should not be read as a format effect.

## Do the results generalise over stimulus exemplars?

Each item class (stimulus × angle) comprises several concrete exemplars. The paper's RT model treats exemplars as interchangeable.
Random intercepts for the exemplar were added.

```{r exemplar-re}
ex_dat <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  filter(correct == 1, trial_number != 1) |>
  mutate(item_group = factor(item_group), stimulus = factor(stimulus), site_label = factor(site_label),
         angle_sc = (angle - mean(angle)) / deg, adaptive = factor(adaptive), age_sc = (age - mean(age)) / yrs)
contrasts(ex_dat$site_label) <- contr.sum(levels(ex_dat$site_label))
contrasts(ex_dat$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(ex_dat$stimulus))
ex_f <- formula(full_mod)
m_ex0 <- lmer(ex_f, ex_dat, REML = FALSE, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
m_ex1 <- update(m_ex0, . ~ . + (1 | item_original))
ex_lrt <- anova(m_ex0, m_ex1)
ex_sd <- attr(VarCorr(m_ex1)$item_original, "stddev")
ex_slopes <- bind_rows(
  slopes(m_ex0, newdata = ex_dat, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "item_group") |> as_tibble() |> mutate(Model = "No exemplar effect"),
  slopes(m_ex1, newdata = ex_dat, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "item_group") |> as_tibble() |> mutate(Model = "Exemplar random intercept"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-exemplar
#| tbl-cap: "**Angle slope (log RT per 40°) with and without exemplar random intercepts.**"
ex_slopes |>
  transmute(Model, Stimulus = toupper(item_group), Slope = fmt3(estimate), SE = fmt3(std.error),
            `95% CI` = ci_str(conf.low, conf.high)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

There are `{r} n_distinct(ex_dat$item_original)` exemplars. Their random intercept has SD = `{r} fmt3(ex_sd)` log units and improves fit
(χ²(1) = `{r} round(ex_lrt$Chisq[2])`, *p* < .001). The angle slopes are unchanged and their standard errors roughly double, so
the angle effect does not depend on the particular exemplars sampled. The SEs from this model are the ones to report.

## Is age linear?

```{r age-nonlinear}
th <- mrot_df |> left_join(sex_data_cleaned, by = "user_id") |> mutate(site_label = factor(site_label))
th_lin <- lmer(metric_value ~ age + site_label + (1 | user_id), th, REML = FALSE)
th_quad <- lmer(metric_value ~ age + I(age^2) + site_label + (1 | user_id), th, REML = FALSE)
th_lrt <- anova(th_lin, th_quad)
th_b <- fixef(th_quad)
th_rate <- \(a) th_b[["age"]] + 2 * th_b[["I(age^2)"]] * a

m_q <- update(full_mod, . ~ . + I(age_sc^2) + angle_sc:I(age_sc^2))
q_lrt <- anova(full_mod, m_q)
sd_theta <- sd(th$metric_value)
```

A quadratic age term improves the ability model (χ²(1) = `{r} fmt2(th_lrt$Chisq[2])`, *p* < .001).
The estimated gain falls from `{r} fmt2(th_rate(5))` θ per year at age 5 to `{r} fmt2(th_rate(9))` at age 9 and `{r} fmt2(th_rate(13))` at age 13.
Adding age² and its interaction with angle to the response-time model also improves fit (χ²(2) = `{r} fmt2(q_lrt$Chisq[2])`,
*p* = `{r} fmt3(q_lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2])`). The pooled SD of θ across assessments is `{r} fmt2(sd_theta)`; it includes between-dataset
differences in mean θ, which is why the paper's 0.33 per year corresponds to `{r} fmt2(0.33 / sd_theta)` SD per year.

## Angle slopes by site, age group and stimulus type

```{r}
#| label: tbl-site-age
#| tbl-cap: "**Angle slope (log RT per 40°) by site, age group and stimulus type** (average marginal effects over observed trials, SE in parentheses; * marks slopes whose 95% CI includes zero)."

sa_dat <- mrot_lme_data |> mutate(age_group = cut(age, age_breaks, right = FALSE))
sa <- slopes(full_mod, newdata = sa_dat, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc",
             by = c("site_label", "item_group", "age_group")) |> as_tibble()
sa |>
  mutate(cell = glue("{fmt3(estimate)} ({fmt3(std.error)}){if_else(conf.low <= 0 & conf.high >= 0, '*', '')}"),
         Stimulus = toupper(item_group)) |>
  select(Site = site_label, Stimulus, age_group, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = age_group, values_from = cell) |>
  arrange(Site, Stimulus) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Slopes increase with age at every site, for both stimulus types. For the youngest children the 3D slope cannot be told apart from zero
at the two Colombian sites (marked), and is small at western-ca. The 2D slope at ages 5--7 is reliably positive everywhere.

# 7. Sex differences

## Ability

```{r sex-theta}
ths <- th |> filter(!is.na(sex)) |> mutate(sex = factor(sex))
contrasts(ths$sex) <- contr.sum(levels(ths$sex))
sx_add <- lmer(metric_value ~ age + site_label + sex + (1 | user_id), ths)
sx_co <- summary(sx_add)$coefficients["sex1", ]
sx_d <- 2 * sx_co[1] / sd(ths$metric_value)           # female minus male, in SD units
sx_hw <- 2 * 1.96 * sx_co[2] / sd(ths$metric_value)   # half-width of the 95% CI
sx_a1 <- lmer(metric_value ~ age * site_label + sex + (1 | user_id), ths, REML = FALSE)
sx_a2 <- lmer(metric_value ~ age * site_label + sex * site_label + (1 | user_id), ths, REML = FALSE)
sx_a_lrt <- anova(sx_a1, sx_a2)
sx_site <- map(levels(ths$site_label), \(s) {
  m <- lm(metric_value ~ age + sex, filter(ths, site_label == s) |> mutate(sex = factor(as.character(sex), levels = c("Female", "Male")))); cc <- summary(m)$coefficients
  r <- str_which(rownames(cc), "^sex")
  tibble(Site = s, `Male − female (SD)` = fmt2(cc[r, 1] / sd(ths$metric_value)),
         `95% CI half-width` = fmt2(1.96 * cc[r, 2] / sd(ths$metric_value)))
}) |> list_rbind()
```

The female minus male difference in θ, adjusting for age and site, is `{r} fmt3(sx_d)` SD (95% CI ±`{r} fmt2(sx_hw)`). Differences larger than about
`{r} fmt2(sx_hw)` SD are therefore excluded, which rules out the d ≈ 0.20 reported in Lauer et al.'s (2019) meta-analysis for children around age 6. The
sex × site interaction is not significant (χ²(`{r} sx_a_lrt$Df[2]`) = `{r} fmt2(sx_a_lrt$Chisq[2])`, *p* = `{r} fmt2(sx_a_lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2])`), but site-level
intervals are wide, so "held across all four sites" should be worded as "no site showed a difference, though each site alone could not exclude moderate effects".

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sex-site
#| tbl-cap: "**Sex difference in ability (male minus female, SD units) within each site, adjusting for age.**"
kable(sx_site, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

## Response time

The paper's sex contrasts average predictions over a balanced grid of angle, stimulus, site and age. Here they are averaged over the
observed trials instead, the weighting the paper argues for elsewhere.

```{r sex-rt}
sx_rt <- inner_join(mrot_lme_data, sex_data_cleaned, by = "user_id") |> filter(!is.na(sex)) |> mutate(sex = factor(sex))
contrasts(sx_rt$sex) <- contr.sum(levels(sx_rt$sex))
sx_mod <- lmer(log_rt ~ angle_sc * stimulus * site_label * age_sc * sex + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
               sx_rt, REML = FALSE, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
sx_cmp <- \(by) avg_comparisons(sx_mod, newdata = sx_rt, re.form = NA, variables = "sex", by = by) |> as_tibble()
sx_tab <- bind_rows(
  sx_cmp("task") |> mutate(Level = "All"),
  sx_cmp("item_group") |> mutate(Level = toupper(item_group)),
  sx_cmp("site_label") |> mutate(Level = site_label))
sx_slope_diff <- slopes(sx_mod, newdata = sx_rt, re.form = NA, variables = "angle_sc", by = "sex",
                        hypothesis = difference ~ pairwise) |> as_tibble()
sx_ss_a <- lmer(log_rt ~ angle_sc * stimulus * site_label * age_sc + sex + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
                sx_rt, REML = FALSE, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
sx_ss_b <- update(sx_ss_a, . ~ . + sex:site_label)
sx_rt_lrt <- anova(sx_ss_a, sx_ss_b)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sex-rt
#| tbl-cap: "**Male minus female difference in log response time, averaged over observed trials.** Negative values mean boys responded faster. The last column is the percentage difference in response time."
sx_tab |>
  transmute(Level, `Estimate` = fmt3(estimate), SE = fmt3(std.error), `95% CI` = ci_str(conf.low, conf.high),
            p = formatC(p.value, format = "f", digits = 3),
            `% RT` = formatC(100 * (exp(estimate) - 1), format = "f", digits = 1)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Averaged over observed trials, boys respond `{r} abs(round(100 * (exp(sx_tab$estimate[1]) - 1), 1))`% faster
(*p* = `{r} fmt3(sx_tab$p.value[1])`), the same as the grid-based figure in the paper, so the weighting makes no difference to this result.
By stimulus type, the 3D contrast has *p* = `{r} fmt3(sx_tab$p.value[sx_tab$Level == "3D"])` here, against .103 in the paper, so the statement that the effect "holds within stimulus type"
depends on the weighting for 3D. All four sites show faster boys, and the sex × site interaction is not significant
(χ²(`{r} sx_rt_lrt$Df[2]`) = `{r} fmt2(sx_rt_lrt$Chisq[2])`, *p* = `{r} fmt2(sx_rt_lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2])`). The sex difference in angle slope is
`{r} fmt3(sx_slope_diff$estimate)` (SE = `{r} fmt3(sx_slope_diff$std.error)`, *p* = `{r} fmt2(sx_slope_diff$p.value)`).
